title: Secret Righteousness, the Lord's Prayer, and Freedom from Worry
summary: Jesus warns against practicing righteousness to be seen, applying the warning to giving, prayer, and fasting, and at the center he teaches his disciples the Lord's Prayer. He then calls them to store up treasure in heaven rather than on earth, to keep their eye sound, and to see that no one can serve both God and money. The chapter closes with the command not to worry about food and clothing, since the Father who feeds the birds and clothes the lilies knows what his children need, and to seek first his kingdom and righteousness.
story:
The Sermon on the Mount continues. Chapter 5 described a righteousness greater than that of the scribes and Pharisees, reaching to the heart in how disciples treat others, and ended with the call to be whole as the Father is whole. Chapter 6 turns to how that righteousness stands before God: acts of devotion done for the Father rather than for an audience, and a life whose treasure, loyalty, and trust are fixed on him. The word Father occurs twelve times in the chapter, more than in any other chapter of Matthew, and it is the key to the whole. Disciples live before a Father who sees in secret, knows what they need before they ask, forgives, feeds, and clothes, and whose kingdom they may seek above everything else.

The chapter has two movements. The first (verses 1 to 18) concerns religious practice and places the Lord's Prayer at the center of the sermon. The second (verses 19 to 34) concerns possessions and anxiety and moves from warning (treasure that decays, a darkened eye, a rival master) to invitation (look at the birds, consider the lilies, seek first the kingdom). Chapter 7 will close the sermon with teaching on judging, asking, the narrow gate, and the call to build on Jesus' words.
historical:
Giving to the poor, prayer, and fasting were the three great practices of Jewish piety in the Second Temple period. The book of Tobit, written in the last centuries before Christ, joins them: prayer with fasting is good, and almsgiving with righteousness (Tobit 12:8). The Mishnah remembers Simeon the Righteous saying that the world stands on three things, the Torah, the temple service, and acts of loving-kindness (m. Avot 1:2), and later rabbinic teaching ranked charity (tsedakah, a word that also means righteousness) among the highest duties. Jesus assumes that his disciples will do all three (‘when you give’, ‘when you pray’, ‘when you fast’) and addresses only their motive and audience.

Prayer had fixed times and forms. Pious Jews recited the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4-9) morning and evening and prayed a series of blessings, later standardized as the Eighteen Benedictions or Amidah, at the times of the temple sacrifices; the Mishnah discusses until what hour each may be said (m. Berakhot 4:1). Standing was the normal posture, so a man caught in a busy street at the hour of prayer would be seen by all. Several phrases of the Lord's Prayer have Jewish parallels. The Kaddish, an Aramaic prayer still said in synagogues, asks that God's great name be magnified and sanctified and that he establish his kingdom in the lifetime of those who pray, though its first-century wording is uncertain. The sixth blessing of the Amidah asks, ‘Forgive us, our Father, for we have sinned.’ The Babylonian Talmud tells how, in a drought, Rabbi Akiva prayed ‘Our Father, our King’ and rain fell (b. Taanit 25b), the origin of the Avinu Malkenu litany. Jakob Petuchowski and Michael Brocke gathered these parallels in The Lord's Prayer and Jewish Liturgy (1978). Fasting was required by the law only on the Day of Atonement, but pious groups fasted more often; a Pharisee in Luke boasts of fasting twice a week (Luke 18:12), and the Didache (8.1), an early Christian manual, tells believers not to fast with ‘the hypocrites’ on Mondays and Thursdays but on Wednesdays and Fridays.

The Lord's Prayer has its own history. Luke gives a shorter form, with the address ‘Father’ and five petitions, in answer to a disciple's request (Luke 11:1-4); Matthew gives a fuller form within the sermon. The Didache (8.2-3) quotes Matthew's form almost exactly, adds a closing doxology, and tells Christians to pray it three times a day, showing that by around AD 100 the prayer was already fixed in the church's daily life. The familiar doxology, ‘for thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever’, is not in the earliest manuscripts of Matthew (Codex Sinaiticus, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae), and the early commentaries on the prayer by Tertullian, Origen, and Cyprian do not include it. It appears first in the Didache in a two-part form (‘yours is the power and the glory forever’), then in a three-part form in later manuscripts such as Codex Washingtonianus, and it passed into the Byzantine text and the King James Version. Its wording draws on David's prayer, “Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the splendor and the majesty” (1 Chronicles 29:11). Most scholars conclude that it arose as the congregation's response when the prayer was said aloud in worship, following the Jewish custom of closing prayers with praise.

The economic sayings of verses 19 to 34 reflect Galilee's village economy. Most people lived close to subsistence, dependent on the harvest, the weather, and the taxes of Herod Antipas and Rome; a failed harvest meant hunger. Wealth was stored as grain in barns (apothēkai, verse 26), as fine garments that moths could ruin, or as coins and valuables hidden in the house or buried, and thieves broke in by ‘digging through’ (diorussō) walls of mud brick or rubble. Rabbinic tradition also knew the saying against anxious hoarding: Rabbi Eliezer the Great taught that whoever has bread in his basket today and asks what he will eat tomorrow is one of those of little faith (b. Sotah 48b).
cultural:
The word hypocrite (hypokritēs) was the ordinary Greek word for a stage actor, one who answered in a play, and by extension a pretender. Matthew uses it thirteen or fourteen times, more than all the other Gospels together. Greek theater was present on the edges of Jesus' world: Herod the Great built theaters in Jerusalem and Caesarea, and Richard Batey (Jesus and the Forgotten City, 1991) suggested that Jesus knew the theater at Sepphoris, four miles from Nazareth, though Jonathan Reed and others date that building later in the first century. Whatever Jesus had seen, the image was clear: religion performed for spectators, with the mask of piety and the applause as the pay. The phrase ‘they already have their full reward’ uses apechō, which in the business papyri means to receive payment in full and give a receipt: the account is settled.

The trumpet of verse 2 is most likely a figure of speech for self-advertisement; no ancient source describes givers literally blowing trumpets. Some connect it with the thirteen trumpet-shaped offering chests (shofarot) in the temple courts (m. Shekalim 6:5), but Jesus speaks of synagogues and streets. Synagogues handled charity in the villages, collecting and distributing to the poor, and a large gift could win public honor, as inscriptions honoring donors show across the Greek and Roman world. The inner room (tameion, verse 6) was the storeroom at the back of a house, often the only room with a door that closed and without windows. Signs of mourning and penitence included going unwashed, leaving the hair unkempt, and putting ashes on the head; the Mishnah lists washing and anointing among things forbidden on the Day of Atonement (m. Yoma 8:1). Anointing the head with olive oil and washing were ordinary daily grooming, so Jesus tells the one who fasts to look as on any normal day.

Behind verses 22 and 23 lies a Hebrew idiom. A ‘good eye’ is a generous one (Proverbs 22:9, literally ‘good of eye’) and an ‘evil eye’ a grudging, stingy one (Deuteronomy 15:9, Proverbs 28:22); Matthew uses the same idiom in 20:15, where the vineyard owner asks, literally, whether the grumbler's eye is evil because he himself is good. Many ancient writers also thought the eye sent out light, so that a darkened interior could blind the eye itself, and Dale Allison has argued that this theory stands behind the saying. The word mammon (verse 24) is Aramaic for wealth or property; it was not the name of a known god, and its personification as a master is Jesus' own. Augustine, who knew Punic from North Africa, remarked that in that language mammon meant gain (On the Sermon on the Mount 2.14.47).

The illustrations of verses 26 to 30 divide the work of a household: sowing, reaping, and gathering into barns were typically men's work in the fields, while laboring over and spinning wool into cloth was typically women's work at home. The birds and the lilies do neither, yet they are fed and clothed. The ‘lilies of the field’ (krina) cannot be identified with a single species; spring in Galilee brings anemones, poppies, and other wildflowers. Dry grass and weeds fueled the small clay household oven (klibanos), since wood was scarce, so the flowers of one day were the fuel of the next. Solomon's splendor was proverbial, as 1 Kings 10 describes, and a hearer would picture the richest robes Israel had ever known.
literary:
The first half of the chapter is one of the most carefully built passages in the Gospels. Verse 1 states the principle: do not practice righteousness before people in order to be seen, or you have no reward from your Father. Three matching paragraphs apply it to giving (2 to 4), prayer (5 and 6), and fasting (16 to 18). Each follows the same pattern: ‘when you…’, ‘do not be like the hypocrites’, a description of their performance, ‘truly I tell you, they already have their full reward’, the right way to do it in secret, and ‘your Father, who sees what is done in secret, will reward you’. Into the middle paragraph Matthew sets a second teaching on prayer (verses 7 and 8), the Lord's Prayer (9 to 13), and a comment on its petition for forgiveness (14 and 15), so that the prayer stands at the center not only of this chapter but, by count of lines, near the center of the whole Sermon on the Mount.

The prayer has an address and six petitions (seven if the last is divided, as Augustine and the Catholic tradition count them). The first three petitions are in the third person, ‘let your name be hallowed, let your kingdom come, let your will be done’, and concern God; the last three are in the first person plural, ‘give us, forgive us, lead us not, deliver us’, and concern the community's needs. The words ‘on earth as it is in heaven’ may qualify only the third petition or all three, and the structure favors the wider reading. The plural ‘our’ and ‘us’ runs throughout, so that even a disciple alone in the inner room prays as one of a family.

The second half (verses 19 to 34) is a chain of short units joined by the theme of undivided loyalty: two treasures (19 to 21), two eyes (22 and 23), two masters (24), and two kinds of seeking (25 to 34). The last unit is built on the command ‘do not worry’ (mē merimnate), which appears three times (verses 25, 31, 34) and frames two arguments from the lesser to the greater: if the Father feeds the birds, will he not feed you; if he clothes the grass, will he not clothe you. The rabbis called this form of argument qal wachomer, from light to heavy. The climax is verse 33, ‘seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness’, and the final verse ends with a proverb of almost wry realism, ‘Today has enough trouble of its own.’ The word righteousness (dikaiosynē) links the chapter's first verse and its climax, and the verb aphanizō links the hypocrites who ‘disfigure’ their faces (verse 16) with the moth and rust that ‘destroy’ earthly treasure (verses 19 and 20).

outline.t: Do not practice righteousness to be seen
Treasure, the eye, and two masters
Do not worry: seek first the kingdom

doctrines.note: Prayer is addressed to a Father who already knows what his children need (verse 8), so it is not a technique for gaining a hearing but trust expressed in words. The Lord's Prayer orders desire: God's name, kingdom, and will first, then bread, forgiveness, and protection. Its plural ‘our’ makes every private prayer an act of the whole family of God.

Giving, prayer, and fasting are acts of worship offered to the Father who sees in secret. When the real audience is other people, the act becomes a performance that has already been paid for. Jesus does not forbid public worship, which Matthew assumes elsewhere (5:16, 18:19-20); he forbids worship aimed at human applause.

Jesus warns against storing up treasure on earth, where it decays and can be stolen, because the heart follows its treasure (verse 21). Money (mammon) is presented as a rival master that demands the service owed to God alone (verse 24). The teaching does not condemn owning or using goods, but it makes generosity and freedom from possessiveness marks of a disciple.

The Father feeds the birds and clothes the grass, and his care for his children is greater still (verses 26 to 30). Providence here is not a promise of comfort but the ground of freedom from anxious striving: disciples work, as the farmers and spinners do, but they need not be ruled by fear of tomorrow.

The kingdom is prayed for (‘Your kingdom come’, verse 10) and sought above every other good (verse 33). It is God's reign breaking into the present through Jesus and awaited in its fullness, and seeking it first reorders every other desire, including the desire for security.

words.note: Hypokritēs, actor, pretender, hypocrite. It occurs about eighteen times in the New Testament, thirteen or fourteen of them in Matthew (the count depends on a variant at 23:14), three in Luke, and once in Mark. In classical Greek it meant a stage actor or an interpreter of oracles; in the Septuagint of Job it describes the godless. Jesus uses it for people whose religion is aimed at an audience. The word does not mean simply someone who fails to live up to his beliefs, but someone whose outward act and inward aim have come apart.

Misthos, wages, pay, reward. It occurs about twenty-nine times in the New Testament, ten in Matthew, and appears five times in this chapter. The same word is used for a laborer's wages (20:8) and for the Father's reward. The hypocrites receive their misthos in full from human applause; the disciple who acts in secret receives it from the Father. Jesus speaks freely of reward, but the reward is the Father's pleasure and presence, not payment for services, and in the parable of the vineyard workers it is given generously beyond what is earned (20:1-16).

Epiousios, translated ‘daily’. It occurs only in the Lord's Prayer (here and Luke 11:3) and is almost unknown elsewhere in Greek; Origen thought the evangelists had coined it (On Prayer 27.7). Proposed meanings include ‘necessary for existence’ (from epi and ousia), ‘for the coming day’ (from hē epiousa, the next day), and ‘for today’. Jerome reported that the Gospel of the Hebrews read mahar, ‘tomorrow's’, but rendered the word supersubstantialem in Matthew and cotidianum in Luke. Whatever its exact sense, ‘this day’ keeps the request modest, like the manna gathered one day at a time (Exodus 16:4).

Opheilēma, debt, what is owed. It occurs only twice in the New Testament (here and Romans 4:4, of wages owed). In Aramaic the word ḥovah could mean both a debt and a sin, and Jewish teaching often pictured sin as a debt owed to God, which explains why Luke's version asks forgiveness of ‘sins’ while keeping ‘everyone who is indebted to us’ (Luke 11:4). The Book of Common Prayer's ‘trespasses’ comes from Tyndale's translation and from verse 14, where Matthew uses paraptōma, a false step.

Peirasmos, test, trial, temptation. It occurs about twenty-one times in the New Testament. It can mean a trial that proves someone, an enticement to sin, or the great final ordeal before the end (Revelation 3:10). Since James 1:13 says God tempts no one to sin, the petition is usually read as ‘do not let us enter into trial that overcomes us’, as Jesus tells the disciples in Gethsemane to pray that they may not enter into temptation (26:41). The noun links this petition to Jesus' own testing in the wilderness in chapter 4.

Mamōnas, wealth, property, from Aramaic mamona. It occurs only four times in the New Testament: here and three times in Luke 16:9-13, where Jesus speaks of ‘unrighteous mammon’. It is attested in Jewish Aramaic texts for money or possessions and carries no inherent evil; it becomes a rival master because it can command trust and service. English literature made Mammon a character: Edmund Spenser's Cave of Mammon in The Faerie Queene (book 2, 1590) and John Milton's fallen angel who first dug gold in Paradise Lost (book 1, 1667).

Merimnaō, to be anxious, worry, care for. It occurs about nineteen times in the New Testament, seven in Matthew, six of them in verses 25 to 34. It can be negative, anxious preoccupation (Luke 10:41), or positive, proper concern for others (1 Corinthians 12:25, Philippians 2:20, where Timothy will ‘genuinely care’ for the church). Jesus forbids the anxious grasping that tries to secure tomorrow by one's own effort and forgets the Father. Paul's “Be anxious for nothing” (Philippians 4:6) uses the same verb and pairs it with an invitation to prayer.

Oligopistos, of little faith. It occurs five times in the New Testament, four of them in Matthew (6:30, 8:26, 14:31, 16:8) and once in Luke's parallel to this verse (Luke 12:28). It is always addressed to disciples, people with real but weak trust, and in Matthew Jesus always follows it with help: he calms the storm, catches the sinking Peter, and explains the bread. It is a rebuke spoken by one who stays with those he rebukes, not a verdict of rejection.

christ:
Jesus teaches his disciples to call God ‘Our Father in heaven’, sharing with them the relationship he himself has with the Father. In Matthew he speaks of ‘My Father’ (7:21, 11:27, 26:39) and of ‘your Father’, but never joins himself with the disciples in ‘our Father’: he gives them the right to pray this way because he is the Son (11:27). The Gospel shows him praying the prayer's petitions himself. In Gethsemane he prays, “My Father, if this cup cannot pass unless I drink it, may Your will be done” (26:42), the very words of the third petition, and he urges the disciples to watch and pray that they may not enter into temptation (26:41). The kingdom whose coming the prayer asks for is breaking in through his ministry and will come in fullness at his return. The forgiveness the disciples ask for is secured by his death, which he describes as his blood ‘poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins’ (26:28), and the deliverance from the evil one is the victory he won in the wilderness (4:1-11) and completed at the cross and resurrection.

His life embodies the rest of the chapter. He practiced the secret prayer he commends, withdrawing to pray alone on a mountain (14:23). He had no place to lay his head (8:20), stored up no treasure on earth, and served one master. When the tempter offered him bread in the wilderness, he answered that man lives by every word from the mouth of God, the trust in the Father's provision he now teaches his disciples. On the cross, stripped of the clothing the Father gives even to the grass, he entrusted himself to God. He is the Son who sought first his Father's kingdom and righteousness, and through him the disciples become children who may bring every need to a Father who already knows it.
interpretation:
The Lord's Prayer is the most commented-on text in the Gospels. The Didache (8.2-3) already prescribed it three times daily. Tertullian's On Prayer (early third century), the first Christian treatise on it, called it a summary of the whole gospel; Origen's On Prayer (around 233) discussed the puzzle of epiousios; and Cyprian's On the Lord's Prayer (252) stressed its plural ‘our’ as a sign of the church's unity. Gregory of Nyssa preached five homilies on it, and John Chrysostom treated it in his homilies on Matthew (Homily 19). Augustine connected its seven petitions with the beatitudes and the gifts of the Spirit (On the Sermon on the Mount, book 2) and taught that the daily prayer ‘forgive us our debts’ cleanses the everyday sins of believers (Enchiridion 71). In the Latin West its eucharistic reading grew from Jerome's supersubstantialem. Thomas Aquinas called it the most perfect of prayers, since it asks for all we rightly desire in the order we should desire it (Summa Theologiae II-II, question 83, article 9), and Teresa of Ávila built much of The Way of Perfection (1566) as a commentary on it, finding in it the whole path of contemplative prayer.

The Reformation catechisms taught it as the pattern of all prayer: Luther's Small and Large Catechisms (1529), which treat our forgiving of others as a sign God attaches to his promise rather than a merit that earns forgiveness; the Heidelberg Catechism (1563, questions 119 to 129); and the Westminster Shorter Catechism (1647, questions 99 to 107). The Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992, paragraphs 2759 to 2865) devotes its final section to it. Simone Weil's essay Concerning the Our Father described learning it in Greek and saying it with complete attention. Jewish scholars have noted how naturally it sits in the prayer world of the synagogue, with its sanctification of the Name, its hope for the kingdom, and its plea for forgiveness (Petuchowski and Brocke, 1978).

The second half of the chapter has had its own readers. Søren Kierkegaard wrote three sets of discourses on the lilies and the birds, including The Lily in the Field and the Bird of the Air (1849) and ‘The Cares of the Pagans’ in Christian Discourses (1848), in which the lily and the bird become teachers of silence, obedience, and joy. The monastic tradition read verses 19 to 34 as a call to voluntary poverty; Protestant readers such as John Wesley, in his discourses on the sermon, read them as a warning against the accumulation of wealth by those who could give it away.

In the Revised Common Lectionary, verses 1 to 6 and 16 to 21 are read on Ash Wednesday in every year, which is why the church begins Lent with the warning against displaying its fasting, and verses 24 to 34 are read on the eighth Sunday after the Epiphany in Year A. The Lord's Prayer is said at nearly every Christian service, and its musical settings range from Byzantine and Slavonic chant to Igor Stravinsky's Otche nash (1926) and Albert Hay Malotte's popular solo setting (1935).
text:
The Lord's Prayer is the passage where English Bibles differ most visibly. Modern versions end verse 13 at ‘deliver us from the evil one’ and put the doxology, ‘For Yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory forever. Amen’, in a footnote, because it is absent from the earliest manuscripts and the earliest commentaries (see the historical note above). The King James Version, following the later Greek manuscripts, prints it in the text. In verse 13 the Greek tou ponērou can be neuter, ‘from evil’ (KJV, and the Latin a malo), or masculine, ‘from the evil one’ (BSB, ESV, NIV), and translations divide accordingly. In verse 12 the earliest manuscripts have the aorist, ‘as we also have forgiven’, while later ones have the present, ‘as we forgive’, matching Luke.

Liturgical versions also differ from Bible translations. The traditional English form's ‘trespasses’ goes back to William Tyndale and the Book of Common Prayer, while Bibles translating Matthew have ‘debts’. The ecumenical text of the English Language Liturgical Consultation (1988) reads ‘Save us from the time of trial and deliver us from evil’. The French Catholic bishops in 2017 changed ‘do not submit us to temptation’ to ‘do not let us enter into temptation’, and the Italian Missal approved in 2019 adopted ‘do not abandon us to temptation’, after Pope Francis said that God does not push people toward temptation; others defended the traditional wording as a faithful rendering of the Greek and a humble plea, and the debate illustrates how translation carries theology.

Other differences come from manuscripts elsewhere in the chapter. In verse 1 later manuscripts and the KJV read ‘alms’ where the earliest have ‘righteousness’. In verses 4, 6, and 18 the KJV's ‘shall reward thee openly’ adds a word absent from the earliest manuscripts. In verse 25 ‘or what you will drink’ is missing from some early witnesses, including Sinaiticus. In verse 33 Sinaiticus and Vaticanus lack ‘of God’ after ‘kingdom’. In verse 28 the first hand of Codex Sinaiticus appears to have read ‘they do not card’ instead of ‘they do not grow’, a reading T. C. Skeat identified in 1938. In verse 27 older versions say one cannot add ‘one cubit unto his stature’ and newer ones ‘a single hour to his life’; the Greek words can mean either, and the context of worry favors the span of life.

teach.big: Disciples live their devotion, their possessions, and their future before a Father who sees in secret, knows their needs, and forgives, so that they are freed from performing for others and from anxious striving to seek his kingdom first.

outline.t: The question is not whether to practice righteousness but for whom: the audience determines the reward.
Giving is an act of mercy done for the Father, so forgetful of itself that the left hand does not know what the right is doing.
Prayer is not performance for people or a technique for getting God's attention; the Father is already present and already knows.
The Lord's Prayer teaches the order of desire: God's name, kingdom, and will first, then daily bread, forgiveness, and protection, prayed together as a family.
Those who ask the Father to cancel their debts cannot keep holding others' debts against them; forgiveness received becomes forgiveness given.
Fasting is a hidden act of devotion, not a display of piety; the one who fasts looks as on any ordinary day.
Where treasure goes, the heart follows; a generous eye fills a life with light, and money cannot share the throne with God.
The Father who feeds birds and clothes flowers cares more for his children, so they may work without being ruled by worry, seek his kingdom first, and live one day at a time.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings are common. The first takes verses 1 to 18 as a ban on public worship or visible good works; Jesus has just told disciples to let their light shine so that people see their good deeds (5:16). The contrast is not public and private but the aim: God's glory or one's own. The second treats the Lord's Prayer either as a formula to be repeated mechanically, which verses 7 and 8 warn against, or as merely a model never to be prayed as written; the church has always done both, praying the words and learning from their order. The third reads verses 14 and 15 as a contract in which our forgiving earns God's; the parable in 18:23-35 shows the master's forgiveness coming first, and the warning falls on those who refuse to pass it on.

With the second half, avoid preaching a prosperity reading of verse 33, as if seeking the kingdom were a method for obtaining wealth; ‘all these things’ are food and clothing, and the promise is the Father's provision of what is needed. Avoid the opposite error of treating the passage as a command to stop working or planning; the birds are fed through their search for food, and Joseph's storing of grain in Egypt was wisdom (Genesis 41). Above all, avoid using ‘do not worry’ as a rebuke to people suffering from anxiety disorders or depression, as if their illness were simply a lack of faith. Jesus addresses anxious grasping for security, and the one he calls ‘of little faith’ he never abandons.
teach.pastoral: This chapter will reach people who live with anxiety, and some whose anxiety is a medical condition. Teach it in a way that never shames them. Jesus' words invite trust in the Father's care; they do not say that anxious feelings are sin or that faithful people do not struggle, and Jesus himself was ‘sorrowful and deeply distressed’ in Gethsemane (26:37). Name plainly that anxiety disorders are real illnesses and that seeing a doctor or counselor is an act of wisdom consistent with trusting God, as using medicine is. Anyone whose worry has turned to thoughts of self-harm should speak to someone at once and contact emergency or crisis services (in the United States, calling or texting 988). The teaching on forgiveness will press on people who have been abused or badly wronged: forgiveness releases the claim to revenge but does not require reconciliation with someone who remains dangerous, silence about crimes, or returning to harm. Those who are poor or out of work should not hear verses 25 to 34 as a suggestion that their need is their fault; the community of disciples is how the Father often answers ‘give us this day our daily bread’.

hard.q: Does verse 15 mean God's forgiveness depends on our forgiving others?
hard.a:
The objection is plain. Jesus says, “But if you do not forgive men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive yours” (verse 15), and the parable of the unforgiving servant ends with the servant handed over to the jailers until he pays (18:34-35). To many readers this sounds like forgiveness earned by our own performance, in tension with the gospel of grace that the Reformers found in Paul. Protestant readers have felt the difficulty most sharply; Luther raised it himself in his Large Catechism (1529). From another side, counselors and advocates for survivors of abuse have objected that this verse has been used to pressure victims to forgive quickly, keep silent, or return to people who harmed them, as if refusing to do so put their own salvation at risk.

The responses agree on more than they differ. Nearly all interpreters note that in the parable of 18:23-35 the king cancels the servant's vast debt first and freely, and the servant is condemned not for failing to earn forgiveness but for refusing to extend what he had received. Augustine (Enchiridion 71) taught that the petition is the daily cleansing of believers' everyday sins, offered on the condition that they forgive. Luther in the Large Catechism called our forgiving a sign God attaches to his promise, a mark and confirmation of forgiveness rather than a satisfaction for sin. Catholic teaching (Catechism of the Catholic Church 2838 to 2845) describes the petition as asking God's mercy while acknowledging that it cannot reach a heart closed to others. Jewish tradition makes the same connection: Ben Sira told his readers to forgive a neighbor so that their own sins would be pardoned when they pray (Sirach 28:2), and the Mishnah teaches that the Day of Atonement does not atone for wrongs against a neighbor until he is appeased (m. Yoma 8:9). Traditions weigh the warning and the priority of grace differently, but none makes forgiving others optional. On the pastoral side, most teachers now distinguish forgiveness, which releases the debt and the claim to revenge, from reconciliation, which requires repentance and trust, and from justice, which may require reporting a crime; the prayer asks for the first and does not require victims to stay in harm's way.

hard.q: Is Jesus saying that worry and anxiety are sins, and is his counsel realistic for people who really lack food or live with anxiety disorders?
hard.a:
The objection comes from two directions. Some Christian teachers have taken ‘do not worry’ as a direct command whose breach is simply sin. Jay Adams, founder of nouthetic counseling (Competent to Counsel, 1970), treated worry largely as a moral and spiritual failure to be confronted with Scripture, and his approach has shaped some church counseling since. Critics, among them many Christian psychologists and psychiatrists, answer that this reading adds guilt to suffering, ignores the bodily and medical causes of anxiety disorders, and has driven people away from help. Skeptical readers raise the other half of the objection: birds do starve and flowers wither unseen, and in a world where children go hungry, telling the poor that the Father will feed them can sound either naive or cruel.

Responses start from the text. The verb merimnaō is not always negative: Paul uses it for proper care for others (1 Corinthians 12:25, Philippians 2:20) and names his own daily ‘concern for all the churches’ (2 Corinthians 11:28). What Jesus forbids is the anxious pursuit of security that makes food and clothing into masters, the ‘seeking after’ of the Gentiles (verse 32), in the context of a warning against serving mammon. Jesus himself was ‘sorrowful and deeply distressed’ in Gethsemane (26:37), Hebrews says he prayed “with loud cries and tears” (Hebrews 5:7), and the Psalms are full of anguished prayers that God receives. The New Testament's answer to anxiety is invitation, not accusation: “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Many pastors and Christian clinicians, across Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant churches, therefore read the passage as an invitation to trust that coexists with medical treatment, and distinguish the anxious grasping Jesus addresses from illness that needs care. On the skeptic's point, interpreters note that Jesus does not promise that no believer will ever go hungry; Matthew 10:29 acknowledges that sparrows fall, and Paul knew hunger (2 Corinthians 11:27). The promise is that the Father knows and cares, and Jesus' own teaching makes his disciples responsible for feeding the hungry (25:35-40). Kierkegaard's discourses on the lilies and the birds read the passage as teaching presence to today rather than denial of need. The problem of suffering in a world under God's care remains a real question, which this passage addresses with trust rather than explanation.
